description: Title card. Teacher prompts: 'Raise your hand if you've ever talked to Siri/Alexa/Google.'
Grid of 8 AI apps (Siri, Netflix, games, camera, ChatGPT, Spotify, Google, filters) reveals one by one. 'Keep your hand up if YouTube/Netflix has suggested something you liked.'
Prompt: 'What other apps do you think use AI?' Accept all answers — no pressure to define AI yet.
Define generative AI: until recently AI sorted/recommended; ~2017 Transformer + Nov 2022 ChatGPT changed it — AI now CREATES (stories, images, music, code).
simplification: We say 'AI learned to create' — really it's pattern-matched generation from massive data.

description: Title card sets up the wow moment: 3 random ingredients → one story.
3 students secretly enter a character, place, and event (manual input or QR-scan from phones).
notes: Two entry modes: remote (QR/phone) or manual classroom keyboard.

description: Real LLM streams the story word by word, weaving the 3 ingredients together. Stay quiet — let the magic land. After: 'How did it know how to do that?'
notes: Replayable — class can run 2–3 times if loving it.

description: Connect the dots: the 3 inputs combined into a PROMPT. Define prompt. Optional 'behind the scenes' panel reveals the actual system/user/assistant messages sent to the AI.
notes: behindTheScenes panel can expand to show the chat-format messages.

description: Animation walks through how each new word is picked based on all words before it. AI doesn't plan the ending first — it predicts ONE word, then the next.
'Is AI a robot, a smart program, or a digital brain?' Class votes by raising hands for each option. All three are partly right.
Real answer: regular programs follow rules someone WROTE. AI learns rules ITSELF from millions of examples — like how you learned to talk by hearing people talk.
Programs = explicit rules someone wrote. AI = patterns learned from data. Define 'program'.
First scenario pair shown side-by-side (e.g. calculator vs cat detector). Class guesses which is which.
Reveal which is rule-based and which is AI. Bike analogy: you can't learn to ride a bike from instructions.
Second scenario pair. Class guesses again.
Reveal — second example reinforces the pattern.
AI learns FROM EXAMPLES — bad/unbalanced examples = bad learning. Define 'bias'. 'If AI only saw golden retrievers, would it recognize a poodle as a dog?'
Title — three areas to compare: how it learns, emotions, creativity. Honest framing: we don't fully know.
Prompt: how does each one learn?
Both learn — brains from living in the world, AI from millions of text examples.
Prompt: does AI have feelings?
AI sounds emotional but doesn't FEEL anything — like an actor who can cry on cue without being sad.
Prompt: is AI creative?
AI remixes patterns from training data. Is that creativity? Open question for the class.
Punchline: AI was inspired by neurons but is ultimately a giant math function — billions of multiplications. Define 'neuron'.
Define LLM = Large Language Model. 'Three words, each matters — we'll break them down one by one.'
GPT-4 trained on TRILLIONS of words. English Wikipedia ≈ 4B words — these models read hundreds of Wikipedias.
simplification: We say 'words' but technically LLMs process tokens — subword pieces. We use 'words' because it's intuitive.

description: Distinguishes LLMs from image/audio AI. Some newer models handle images too, but language is core.
Mathematical representation of patterns. Analogy: hearing enough songs builds a 'model' of music in your brain — LLMs build a model of language.
Unpack: LLMs aren't just text anymore — vision, audio. Define 'multimodal'. Discussion: 'most popular thing people use LLMs for?'
Auto-scrolling cards: ChatGPT (OpenAI), Claude (Anthropic), Llama (Meta — open source), Gemini (Google). 'Has anyone heard of any of these?'
'BILLIONS of words — but HOW does that teach it to write?' Dramatic pause. Don't answer yet.
Title — AI learns by guessing, being told if it's right or wrong, and adjusting its settings.
Round 1 setup: knock-knock. Cat says 'Lettuce' — what's the punchline? Robots make wild guesses.
Punchline reveals: 'Lettuce in!' Robots got it wrong. Their weight dials shift.
Weight dials represent the BILLIONS of internal numbers. When AI is wrong, those numbers shift slightly. Define 'weights'.
Second round: robots try again with adjusted weights, getting closer.
Reveal whether robots got it right; dials adjust again.
Third round: robots now answer correctly — the learning curve.
Real AI does this MILLIONS of times with millions of examples. It learns the PATTERN, not specific answers.
Transition beat: 'We know what LLMs are. Now we open the hood and look at the engine.' Define 'training'.
simplification: Training stages presented as sequential are actually simultaneous in real training.

description: Robot with crank processes 'The cat sat on the ___' through 96 layers. Don't talk over it — let kids watch.
simplification: 96 layers is GPT-3 specific. GPT-2 has 48; smaller models have 12; newer can have 128+.

description: Punchline: all that work — JUST FOR ONE WORD. Then it does it again. Word by word. That's how AI writes.
Show the word 'cat'. 'When you see this word, what happens in your brain?' Give 30–60s for kids to share.
Capture kids' descriptions: fur, whiskers, purring. Write a few on the board.
Pivot: 'All of that — fur, purring, picture in your head — your brain does instantly. AI can't do ANY of that. Only numbers.' Define 'embedding'.
simplification: AI processes 'tokens' (subword pieces), not whole words. We simplify to 'words'.

description: Numbers stream by, scrolling counter ticks up. Stay quiet — let the visual do the work. 'How many numbers do you think represent one word?'
simplification: 12,288 is GPT-3's embedding dim. GPT-2 uses 768/1,600. Not universal.

description: Each word becomes a point in 'meaning space'. Define 'vector' — coordinates with thousands of dimensions.
Similar meanings = close in space. Kids tap words, connection lines reveal relationships.
Free exploration on the scatter plot. Why are king/queen close but far from pizza?
Words cluster by meaning (animals, vehicles, royalty). AI discovers these clusters from data.
Each dimension captures one aspect of meaning. First named dimension revealed; class names it before reveal.
Cross-category surprise — bird AND plane have wings. AI discovered this on its own.
Another dimension stacks on top.
More dimensions added — DimensionExplorer visualizes scoring.
Real AI uses thousands of dimensions to capture everything about a word's meaning.
simplification: Named dimensions ('Is Animal?') are illustrative. Real dimensions aren't human-readable categories.

description: Show 'bat'. Show of hands: baseball bat or flying bat? Both should get votes.
AI must figure it out without the picture in their head. How would YOU explain which bat using only words?
AI sees BOTH meanings at once... unless it looks at the other words. Sets up the cliffhanger.
Define 'attention' — the process where each word looks at all other words for clues.
Sentence: '...he swung the bat and hit the ball.' Beams light up clue words (swung, hit, ball). Class predicts which words are clues before reveal.
Sentence: '...the bat flew out of the cave at dusk.' Different beams (flew, cave, dusk). Same word, different clues.
That's attention! Multiple attention HEADS work in parallel. Define 'attention head'.
simplification: Real attention is more parallel — each head computes weighted scores for every word pair simultaneously, with many heads per layer.

description: Attention is reading the room and finding relationships. MLP is the THINKING layer — flips through everything ever learned. Define 'MLP'.
simplification: '21 questions' analogy is illustrative — MLP does matrix multiplications, not literal yes/no questions.

description: 21 questions → 49,152 questions. 4× expansion = room to brainstorm. 'Why would you make it bigger in the middle?'
simplification: 4× expansion is GPT-3-style; some models use 8/3× (Llama). Pattern is consistent though.

description: Keep what's useful, throw away the rest. Expand-then-compress = brainstorm then decide. Like deep breath before a hard answer.
Every single layer does BOTH: Attention (words look at each other) + MLP (asks questions). 'How many layers?' (96)
Many layers, each pass richer. Early layers = letters/spelling, middle = grammar/facts, late = reasoning. Class guesses early-vs-late before reveal. Define 'layer'.
simplification: 96 layers is GPT-3; GPT-2 has 48, smaller models 12-24. Layer specialization is gradual, not as clean as 6 ranges.

description: Animation runs through all 96 layers — questions evolve from 'is this spelled right?' (early) to 'which word fits best?' (late). Let it play.
simplification: Flashing questions are an analogy — each layer does math transformations, not literal questions.

description: Big question: all that work — but how does it actually pick the next word? This is the payoff.
Each word sends meaning into the last position. Grammar, facts, context all accumulate. Define 'prediction'.
simplification: By final layer, info is mixed/transformed — not a simple sum of parts. Beam animation oversimplifies.

description: Ranked list: mat 42%, floor 18%, etc. Top word wins — unless temperature adds randomness. Define 'probability'.
simplification: Real distribution is over 50K+ tokens; most get near-zero probability. Numbers shown are illustrative.

description: Generate sentence at temp 0.1 (frozen), then 1.5 (wild). Same prompt, different results. Define 'temperature'.
Words → Numbers → Space → Attention → MLP → Predict. 'Now that you know how AI works — does it change how you'd use it?'
Three tools: Predict, Word Space, Generate. Kids get to use real AI and see the concepts in action.
Tabbed playground: Predict (real probability rankings), Word Space (real embeddings plotted), Generate (streaming AI writing word by word). Take turns suggesting prompts.
notes: Uses gpt-4o-mini + text-embedding-3-small. Embedding viz uses PCA to 2D — loses most information.
